newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai markets anxiously await economic package.
newsitem.headline: Thai markets anxiously await economic package.

text.p: Thailand's markets are anxiously awaiting a promised economic rescue package due to be presented by the government on Tuesday, analysts and dealers said.

Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya has said he will announce a raft of measures, likely to include tough steps recommended by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), to help tackle the country's severe economic crisis.

The Thai government's pledge to involve the IMF in the prescriptive measures helped support equity and currency markets last week as the possibility of IMF participation was seen as lending credibility to the package, analysts said. But it is still not clear if the package will include IMF loans or standby credit lines.
Japanese banks have so far linked a loan to Thailand to the IMF's involvement in the rescue plans.

Japan's Nihon Keizai Shimbun financial newspaper reported on Sunday that the Export-Import Bank of Japan and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have put together an $8 billion emergency loan package for Thailand, to be unveiled after the restructuring plan is announced.
Dealers and analysts said Thailand's stock and currency markets would start next week cautiously before the package is announced and then react to its contents. But stocks could move down.

"I think it sets people up for more downside than upside because almost everything positive you could hope for is already out in the market," said Russell Kopp, head of research at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
The Thai stock market's SET Index ended the week at 652.04, down 1.31 points from the previous week's close.
The baht ended at 31.90/32.00 per dollar against the previous Friday's close of 32.05/32.20.

The IMF's backing is seen as crucial for the package to appeal to investors, but some fears persist as to whether the IMF will have much of a role in addressing Thailand's growing problems, analysts said.
The Thai economy is reeling under the pressures of a slowdown in exports, a weak stock market and problems in the financial sector linked to over-exposure to the ailing real estate market.
Thailand last month floated the baht after years of tying it to a fixed basket of currencies, resulting in a de facto devaluation, after repeated attacks on the currency by speculators.
On Friday, rating agency Standard and Poor's put Thailand's long term "A" foreign currency rating on negative watch and put a series of other ratings under negative review.

"All eyes are clearly on the package. We will wait to see what agreement has been reached and what role the IMF is to play. At the moment there are still doubts that this could be strung out for a while longer," said a senior foreign analyst.
Confidence that the IMF would be given a free hand has been undermined by fears that authorities would be reluctant to reveal the extent of the economy's woes.

Such concerns over transparency have been heightened by the revelation last week that one of Thailand's largest electronics companies, Alphatec Electronics Plc, had been concealing a 10-billion baht ($322-million) hole in its accounts last week.

"There is this real sense that there is so much hiding under the carpet. If the IMF comes in it is going to force Thailand to lift up the carpet and find out what is under there," said one local fund manager affiliated with a Thai commercial bank.
The sense of unease, particularly among some foreign investors, has been heightened by unexpectedly high central bank foreign reserve figures announced on Thursday.
They showed the bank's reserve figures fell only $900 million to $32.4 billion in June from $33.3 billion in May despite heavy intervention in markets in the run up to the baht's July 2 floatation.
"It has left people wondering why they devalued and why the capital controls remain in place if the reserves are this high," said one foreign analyst.
Political manoeuvring has also caused some concerns. A number of high-level changes last week were widely seen as shoring up Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's power base.

The government forced the removal of outspoken finance ministry civil servant Chatumongol Sonakul last week, heightening speculation that elements in the administration were seeking to close ranks prior to any IMF involvement, analysts said.
